David becomes king over Israel (verses 1–9)

David came to occupy Israel's throne after reigning for seven years in Hebron over Judah alone.

God's purposes will be fulfilled at last, whatever obstacles stand in the way.

True greatness consists in being genuinely useful and dedicating all our abilities to the Lord.

David's mighty men (verses 10–47)

This passage records the distinguished men who served David.

Yet David attributed his success not to the mighty men with him but to the mighty God, whose presence matters more than anything else.

By strengthening David, these men also strengthened themselves and advanced their own interests, because his advancement benefited them.

We likewise gain by doing what we can, in the places God gives us, to support the kingdom of the Son of David.

Those faithful to Christ will find their names recorded with far greater honor than these men's names in the records of earthly fame.

David was brought to possess the throne of Israel after he had reigned seven years in Hebron, over Judah only. God's counsels will be fulfilled at last, whatever difficulties lie in the way. The way to be truly great, is to be really useful, to devote all our talents to the Lord.
[1Chr.11.10-1Chr.11.47]
Verses 10-47
An account is given of David's worthies, the great men who served him. Yet David reckoned his success, not as from the mighty men that were with him, but from the mighty God, whose presence is all in all. In strengthening him, they strengthened themselves and their own interest, for his advancement was theirs. We shall gain by what we do in our places for the support of the kingdom of the Son of David; and those that are faithful to Him, shall find their names registered much more to their honour, than these are in the records of fame.

Those who joined David at Ziklag (verses 1–22)

This is an account of people who openly befriended and supported David while he was being persecuted.

Neither difficulty nor danger should keep a sinner from coming to the Savior or drive a believer away from the path of duty.

Those who press through such obstacles and overcome them will receive an abundant reward.

Amasai's words teach us how to express our love and loyalty to the Lord Jesus: we must belong entirely to him and be ready to stand and act on his side.

When the Spirit rules our hearts, we want to belong among Christ's people and declare ourselves on their side.

When faith and love move us to embrace Christ's cause, he receives us, employs us and advances us.

Those who joined David at Hebron (verses 23–40)

When Christ's throne is established in a person's soul, there is—or ought to be—great joy.

There is also provision for that soul, not merely for the few days described here but for all of life and throughout eternity.

Happy are those who wisely recognize that submitting to Jesus Christ, the Son of David, is both their duty and their best interest.

They abandon whatever is incompatible with allegiance to him.

Their efforts to do good are guided by the wisdom God gives through his word, experience and observation.

If any of us lacks that wisdom, let us ask God. He gives generously to everyone without reproach, and the wisdom will be given.

Here is an account of those who appeared and acted as David's friends, while he was persecuted. No difficulties or dangers should keep the sinner from coming to the Savior, nor drive the believer from the path of duty. Those who break through, and overcome in these attempts, will find abundant recompence. From the words of Amasai we may learn how to testify our affection and allegiance to the Lord Jesus; his we must be throughly; on his side we must be forward to appear and act. If we are under the influence of the Spirit, we shall desire to have our lot among them, and to declare ourselves on their side; if in faith and love we embrace the cause of Christ, he will receive, employ, and advance us.
[1Chr.12.23-1Chr.12.40]

When the throne of Christ is set up in a soul, there is, or ought to be, great joy in that soul; and provision is made, not as here, for a few days, but for the whole life, and for eternity. Happy are those who wisely perceive it to be their duty and interest, to submit to the Saviour Jesus Christ, the Son of David; who renounce for his sake all that is not consistent; whose earnest endeavours to do good are directed by the wisdom that God giveth, through acquaintance with his word, experience, and observation. If any man lack this wisdom, let him ask it of God, who giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not, and it shall be given him.

David consults about the ark (verses 1–5)

David did not ask what magnificent or pleasurable thing he should now do. He asked what godly thing he should do, so that he might enjoy the comfort and benefit of God's sacred oracle.

He wanted the ark brought among the people to be a blessing to them.

Those who honor God also do what truly benefits themselves.

People beginning their lives in the world act wisely when they bring God's ark with them.

Those who begin with reverence for God are well placed to continue enjoying his favor.

The removal of the ark and Uzza's death (verses 6–14)

Uzza's sin warns us to avoid presumption, rashness and irreverence when approaching holy things.

A good intention never makes a wrong action right.

His punishment teaches us not to treat God lightly when we approach him.

Yet through Jesus Christ we may come boldly to the throne of grace.

The ark brought death to Uzza; similarly, for some the gospel is an aroma leading from death to death.

But when we welcome the gospel with love for its truth, it becomes an aroma leading from life to life.

Let us bring the ark to us, that it may be a blessing to us. Those who honour God, profit themselves. It is the wisdom of those setting out in the world, to take God's ark with them. Let the sin of Uzza warn all to take heed of presumption, rashness, and irreverence, in dealing with holy things; and let none think that a good design will justify a bad action. Let the punishment of Uzza teach us not to dare to trifle with God in our approaches to him; yet let us, through Christ, come boldly to the throne of grace. If the gospel be to some a savour of death unto death, as the ark was to Uzza, yet let us receive it in the love of it, and it will be to us a savour of life unto life.

David's victories

This chapter records three things: David's kingdom being established, his family being built up, and his enemies being defeated.

The account repeats events recorded in 2 Samuel 5.

David's reputation and fame point toward the far greater exalted honor of the Son of David, Jesus Christ.

Preparing to bring the ark (verses 1–24)

Even wise and godly people can make mistakes. When they become aware of them, they should correct them.

David did not try to justify what had been done wrongly or blame others.

He acknowledged that he, together with others, had failed to seek God in the proper order.

The ark is brought to Jerusalem (verses 25–29)

We should recognize God's providential help even in activities that are naturally within our abilities.

Without his assistance, we could not take a single step.

Whenever we fulfill a religious duty rightly, even to a small degree, we must acknowledge that God helped us. Left to ourselves, we would have made serious errors.

Everything we undertake must be done in dependence on God's mercy through the Redeemer's sacrifice.

[1Chr.15.25-1Chr.15.29]

It is good to notice the assistance of Divine Providence, even in things which fall within the compass of our natural powers; if God did not help us, we could not stir a step. If we do our religious duties in any degree aright, we must own it was God that helped us; had we been left to ourselves, we should have been guilty of some fatal errors. And every thing in which we engage, must be done in dependence on the mercy of God through the sacrifice of the Redeemer.

The ark is established (verses 1–6)

God's word and appointed ordinances may seem clouded or eclipsed for a time, but they will shine again after that obscurity.

The ark was housed only in a tent, a humble dwelling. Yet David spoke of that tabernacle with deep affection throughout his psalms.

God had been gracious to David, and David now showed generosity toward his people.

Those whose hearts have expanded with holy joy should show that joy through openhanded generosity.

David's psalm of praise (verses 7–36)

Let our praise bring glory to God, while also teaching and encouraging other people, so that even strangers to him may learn to worship him.

Let us rejoice in the Lord and trust him. People who give glory to God's name may rightly rejoice in that name.

God's everlasting covenant should be the great source of our joy. We should remember it with thanksgiving, as his people did in earlier times.

Day by day, announce his salvation—the salvation promised through Jesus Christ.

We have reason to celebrate it every day because we receive its benefits daily, and the subject can never be exhausted.

Even in the midst of praise, do not forget to pray for God's servants who are suffering.

Worship is organized (verses 37–43)

Worshiping God should be part of every day. David established an orderly pattern.

At Jerusalem, where the ark stood, Asaph and his companions ministered continually with songs of praise.

No sacrifices or incense were offered there because the altars were elsewhere.

Yet David's prayers rose like incense, and his raised hands were like the evening sacrifice. Spiritual worship was already taking the place of ceremonial worship in this respect.

Still, God had instituted the ceremonial ordinances, so they must not be neglected.

At Gibeon, where the altars stood, the priests continued offering sacrifices and incense morning and evening, in accordance with Moses' law.

Those ceremonies pictured the mediation of Christ, making their appointed observance important.

The faithful presence of ministers whom God appoints is right in itself and encourages the people.

Verses 1-6
Though God's word and ordinances may be clouded and eclipsed for a time, they shall shine out of obscurity. This was but a tent, a humble dwelling, yet this was the tabernacle which David, in his psalms, often speaks of with so much affection. David showed himself generous to his subjects, as he had found God gracious to him. Those whose hearts are enlarged with holy joy, should show it by being open-handed.
[1Chr.16.7-1Chr.16.36]
Verses 7-36
Let God be glorified in our praises. Let others be edified and taught, that strangers to him may be led to adore him. Let us ourselves triumph and trust in God. Those that give glory to God's name are allowed to glory in it. Let the everlasting covenant be the great matter of our joy his people of old, be remembered by us with thankfulness to him. Show forth from day to day his salvation, his promised salvation by Christ. We have reason to celebrate that from day to day; for we daily receive the benefit, and it is a subject that can never be exhausted. In the midst of praises, we must not forget to pray for the servants of God in distress.
[1Chr.16.37-1Chr.16.43]
Verses 37-43
The worship of God ought to be the work of every day. David put it into order. At Jerusalem, where the ark was, Asaph and his brethren were to minister before the ark continually, with songs of praise. No sacrifices were offered there, nor incense burnt, because the altars were not there; but David's prayers were directed as incense, and the lifting up of his hands as the evening sacrifice. So early did spiritual worship take place of ceremonial. Yet the ceremonial worship, being of Divine institution, must by no means be omitted; therefore at Gibeon, at the altars, the priests attended; for their work was to sacrifice and burn incense; and that they did continually, morning and evening, according to the law of Moses. As the ceremonies were types of the mediation of Christ, the observance of them was of great consequence. The attendance of his appointed ministers is right in itself, and encourages the people.

modern_osis:
Original heading

David's purposes; God's gracious promises.

God's promise to David

This chapter repeats the account in 2 Samuel 7. The comments on that chapter also apply here.

There is, however, a notable difference in wording: what Samuel calls “for your word's sake” is described here as “for your servant's sake” (verse 19).

Jesus Christ is both the Word of God (Revelation 19:13) and the Servant of God (Isaiah 42:1).

God fulfills his promises to all believers for Christ's sake and because of his mediation. In him, every promise is Yes and Amen.

For his sake the promises are fulfilled and made known. We owe all this greatness to him and look to him for the great things still to come.

These are the unsearchable riches of Christ.

If through faith we recognize their worth, both in themselves and in the Lord Jesus, we cannot help praising them as the only true greatness and speaking honorably of them.

May we seek this blessedness through life's trials, when we feel death approaching, and for the children who come after us.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.17.1]
Chapter 17
David's purposes; God's gracious promises.
--This chapter is the same as 2Sa 7. See what is there said upon it. It is very observable that what in Samuel is said to be, "for thy word's sake," is here said to be, "for thy servant's sake," ver. #(19). Jesus Christ is both the Word of God, [Rev.19.13] Re 19:13, and the Servant of God, [Isa.42.1] Is 42:1; and it is for his sake, upon account of his mediation, that the promises are made good to all believers; it is in him, that they are yea and amen. For His sake it is done, for his sake it is made known; to him we owe all this greatness, from him we are to expect all these great things. They are the unsearchable riches of Christ, which, if by faith we see in themselves, and see in the Lord Jesus, we cannot but magnify as the only true greatness, and speak honourably of them. For this blessedness may we look amidst the trials of life, and when we feel the hand of death upon us; and seek it for our children after us.

David's victories

This chapter repeats the events recorded in 2 Samuel 8.

Our good fight of faith, under the Captain of our salvation, will end in everlasting triumph and peace.

The happiness of Israel through David's victories and his just government was only a faint picture of the happiness awaiting God's redeemed people in heaven.

David's wars

This chapter repeats the history recorded in 2 Samuel 10.

A sinner's only safety is to submit to the Lord, seek peace with him and become his servant.

We should help one another in a good cause.

But let us be careful: we may be used as instruments of good for others and yet, through unbelief and sin, fail to receive salvation ourselves.

David's wars

The Lord may severely correct the sins of his believing people, but he will not abandon them to their enemies.

His help will overcome every advantage in numbers and strength held by those who oppose his Israel.

Everyone who trusts in Christ will become more than a conqueror through the One who loves them.
